title: Microsoft Copilot Studio
subtitle: I expose a trimmed, authenticated tool surface to Microsoft Copilot Studio through an edge proxy, and worked out from the wire why its connector stalled after initialisation.

stats.label: tools for desktop assistants, over a local transport

lede: I wanted Microsoft Copilot Studio agents to call tools on my private MCP server in the Auth and access plane, and I wanted that server to accept no public connection. The standard MCP OAuth path stalled right after initialize , and Copilot Studio's MCP connector was thinly documented. I decided to work out its behaviour from the wire and build around what it actually does. I read the connector's traffic end to end in edge logs and wrote it down as observed fact, which made each proxy decision traceable to something the connector does. From that I built a small edge proxy.
quote: When a vendor platform is under-documented, I learn it from the wire.
evidence: Reverse-engineering vendor integrations: Copilot Studio's MCP connector behaviour worked out from edge logs and answered by an edge proxy of about 300 lines.
Zero-trust and zero-inbound networking: a private tool server reachable only through a tunnel, with tenant-pinned Entra token checks at the edge.
MCP tool surface design: 21 tools for desktop assistants and a trimmed 8-tool surface shaped for Copilot Studio.
author: Corey James
